extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, and medical researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and arguments about adopting open (non-anonymous) peer review in medical journals — identifying reviewers to authors and ultimately making the review record public. Discusses evidence, ethical reasoning, benefits, and risks for implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify reviewers to authors (open reviewer identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ will identify to authors the names of those who have reviewed their papers, including in-house editorial and statistical advisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented for all new papers as a first step. Evidence from a randomized trial showed open peer review did not change review quality, so the move is justified largely on ethical grounds. Reviewers may decline to review if they do not wish to be identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability of the peer review record (full transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Soon we are likely to open up the whole system so that anybody interested can see the whole process on the world wide web.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible next steps include listing reviewers at the end of articles and creating a system where authors and readers can watch the peer review system on the web as it happens and contribute comments, making peer review an ongoing scientific discourse rather than a summary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking reviewer identity to accountability and duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying the reviewer links 'privilege and duty, by reminding the reviewer that with power comes responsibility: that the scientist invested with the mantle of the judge cannot be arbitrary in his or her judgment and must be a constructive critic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openness is argued to reduce curt, abusive, or destructive reviews because the reviewer is known; it should remind reviewers to be constructive and responsible in their judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give reviewers academic credit and recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Openness links accountability with credit. One important defect of closed review is that reviewers don’t receive academic credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing reviewer names or making reviews visible should help reviewers receive recognition for their work, addressing the lack of academic credit in closed review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce abuses such as idea theft and procrastination
rubrics_metrics.description: Openness should eliminate some of the worst abuses of peer review, where reviewers—under the cloak of anonymity—steal ideas or procrastinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making reviewer identity and/or reviews public is expected to deter theft of ideas and reduce procrastination and other abusive behaviors enabled by anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect the ability of junior reviewers to critique senior researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: The main argument against open peer review is that junior reviewers will be reluctant to criticise the work of senior researchers for fear of reprisals; by moving to open review we may thus be ruling out the best reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise this trade-off. Allow reviewers to decline particular reviews if they do not wish to be identified; pursue culture change to reduce fear of reprisals and preserve contributions from junior reviewers, who have repeatedly been shown to give excellent opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt changes based on evidence and ongoing research
rubrics_metrics.description: The change to open review is based on evidence and an ethical argument. Randomised trials have been used to test blinding and open review effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research as you go: use randomized trials and other evidence to evaluate effects (e.g., studies showing blinding had mixed effects and that open review did not reduce review quality). Policy changes should be informed by such evidence while also considering ethical factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge peer review's primary function: improving published work
rubrics_metrics.description: The benefits of peer review are harder to pin down, but it is probably more useful for improving what is eventually published than for sorting the wheat from the chaff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate peer review systems by their contribution to improving manuscripts and the published record, not solely by their filtering ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise known defects of conventional peer review to target improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is slow, expensive, profligate of academic time, highly subjective, prone to bias, easily abused, poor at detecting gross defects, and almost useless for detecting fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms should aim to address these specific problems (speed, cost, subjectivity, bias, susceptibility to abuse, poor error/fraud detection) when designing alternative peer review models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow reviewer opt-out and phased implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: A few reviewers have said that they don’t want to review if they will be identified, and anyone can decline to review a particular paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce openness gradually (identify reviewers to authors first, then list reviewers publicly, then consider live web-based review) while allowing reviewers to opt out of particular assignments to respect individual concerns during transition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include editorial and statistical advisers transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ will identify to authors the names of those who have reviewed their papers, including the names of our in house editorial and statistical advisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency should cover all contributors to the review process (including in-house advisors), not only external reviewers, to give a fuller picture of who influenced editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster peer review as a public scientific discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review will become increasingly a scientific discourse rather than a summary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems (e.g., web-based open records and reader contributions) that enable ongoing discussion around manuscripts, allowing authors, readers, and reviewers to interact and contribute to the evaluation and improvement of work.
